solution:
Almost, but not quite. The chapter says tertiary activities are mostly in the form of services, and that because these activities are mainly of the service category the sector is also known as the service sector.

The qualification it adds is that in tertiary occupations there is no derivation from nature as in primary activities, and there may be some products manufactured as in secondary activities, but they are in the form of services offered.

So the sector is defined by the service rather than by the absence of any product. Buying and selling of goods, loading and unloading, marketing, import and export all handle goods without producing them.

Yes, but the product is incidental to the service.

The chapter states that there may be some products manufactured like in secondary activities, but that they are in the form of services offered.

Examples from the chapter's own list of tertiary activities show what it means. Print, films, radio and television produce something a person can hold or watch, yet the activity is broadcasting or publishing, which is a service. A bank issues a passbook and an insurer a policy, but what is sold is banking and insurance. A postal service carries a letter it did not write.

The test is where the value comes from. In a secondary activity the value is in the object made; in a tertiary one it is in the service, and any object is the vehicle for it.

| Dependent on geographical factors | Not dependent on geographical factors |
|---|---|
| Rail network | Banking |
| Road network | Insurance |
| Waterways | Real estate |
| Airways | Print |
| Pipeline | Landline |
| Ports and loading and unloading of goods | Mobile |
| Tourism | Films |
| Rural wholesale mandies | Radio |
| Urban wholesale markets | Television |
| Periodic markets | Postal services |
| Retail trade: stores, shops, malls, chain stores, street peddling | Personal and professional services |
| Public Distribution System (PDS) | |

The chapter's own conclusion is that there are very few such services which are not dependent on natural factors completely, so the right-hand column should be read as less dependent rather than independent.

The factors it names are climate, topography, nearness to the sea and continental location. Transport is the clearest case: relief, location and climate are the three major physical factors governing it, rails and roads are easier to build where relief is not rugged, and only broken coastlines make good ports.

Markets are the second clear case. The chapter states that human settlements have developed as an effect of favourable geographical factors, that markets always occur near these settlements, and that while a secondary activity can occur away from settlements, markets will not.

Tourism is the third, since the chapter names site and situation, climate, relief, altitude, biodiversity, accessibility and availability of water among the physical factors in its growth.

Almost everything in daily use has passed through all three kinds of activity, which is the point of the exercise.

Taking a few examples the chapter's own categories supply:

| Thing used | Primary | Secondary | Tertiary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salt | Obtained from sea water or rock salt | Refined and packed | Carried, wholesaled and retailed to the shop |
| Bread | Wheat grown | Milled into flour and baked | Transported and sold |
| A cotton shirt | Raw cotton grown | Spun, woven and stitched | Wholesale and retail trade |
| Electricity | Coal mined or water impounded | Generated at a power station | Transmitted and billed |
| A mobile phone | Minerals mined | Components made and assembled | Sold, and the network service provided |

The chapter's framing explains the pattern. Primary activities obtain natural resources; some products cannot be used directly and are processed, which makes them secondary; and there are activities which act as the link between the two and are complementary to both, mostly in the form of services.

That is why almost nothing on such a list escapes the third column. Even a product taken straight from nature reaches the user through buying and selling, transport and loading and unloading, all of which are tertiary.

Yes, trade can take place, even though both countries produce the same crop.

The reason is efficiency rather than variety. A produces 500 tonnes of wheat with 200 labourers, that is 2.5 tonnes per labourer; B produces 1,000 tonnes with 300 labourers, that is about 3.3 tonnes per labourer. B is the more efficient producer and has a surplus to sell.

The chapter's principle covers this: international trade occurs when it is mutually beneficial to trading partners and when it is a comparative advantage for both, rather than producing in their own countries. It adds that international trade is a result of specialisation in production and human resources.

Yes, and this is the clearer of the two cases.

C produces 300 kg of tea and no coffee; D produces 500 kg of coffee and no tea. Each has what the other lacks, so each can supply the other's want.

The chapter's first geographical factor explains why such a difference exists at all: the natural resources available in one country will be different from those available in another, and soil, minerals, forests, land, water and human resources are unevenly distributed. It gives the parallel case of the Gulf countries, which are rich in mineral oil and so export oil but import grains.

It tells us that the two economies differ in productivity rather than in what they can produce.

Both grow wheat, so neither has a resource the other lacks. What differs is output per worker: 2.5 tonnes in A against about 3.3 tonnes in B. B is therefore likely to have better land, better technology or better organisation, and A to have surplus labour employed at lower productivity.

The chapter's terms for this are specialisation and comparative advantage: international trade is a result of specialisation in production and human resources, and it occurs when it is a comparative advantage for both rather than producing in their own countries. B specialises in wheat and A is better employed elsewhere.

It tells us that the two countries have different climates.

The chapter states that climate affects the plants and animals in a region and ensures how different types of products can be grown or produced in a country. Tea and coffee need different conditions, so a country that grows one and not the other is telling us about its climate.

Its own example is exactly this: tropical countries produce and export bananas, rice, cocoa, tea and coffee, and Sri Lanka is a major tea exporter because cheap labour, a favourable climate, undulating land and soil which can drain water make tea plantations possible on a large scale there. The United Kingdom has no tea plantations but a high demand for tea, so India and Sri Lanka export tea to it.

It tells us that the two countries have specialised their human resources in different directions, and that trade can be in services as much as in goods.

Country E has expertise in water engineering and agriculture; country F in metro-making. Neither is a natural resource; both are skills.

The chapter treats this as a factor in its own right. Under specialisation it says some countries have specialised goods and services, and gives Israel, which has specialised in dry farming or agricultural engineering and so exports its services to countries wishing to carry out agriculture in desert-like conditions. It adds that specialised goods and services have an international demand and therefore trade may occur between countries.

It also lists international trade as a result of specialisation in production AND human resources, which is the half this condition illustrates.

The chapter lists five geographical factors affecting trade.

Difference in natural resources. Each region differs from another, and soil, minerals, forests, land, water and human resources are unevenly distributed, so what is abundant in one country is scarce in another. A country rich in soil is a good exporter of grains; the Gulf countries, rich in mineral oil, export oil and import grains.

Climate. Climate affects the plants and animals of a region and decides what can be grown or produced. Snow-covered countries export meat and woollen products; tropical countries export bananas, rice, cocoa, tea and coffee.

Population factors. The size, distribution and diversity of people differ between countries.

Specialisation. Some countries have specialised goods and services, such as Israel's dry farming and agricultural engineering, and such goods and services have an international demand.

Government policies. These may cause or stop international trade; a free trade policy will not restrict citizens from buying or selling to another country, and a country may trade with another to maintain good relations.

To these the chapter adds transport, which it treats under a heading of its own: transportation is a very important tertiary activity for trading, and the importance of ports, sea transport and air transport has been very obvious in trade.

Table 1 shows the direct contribution of travel and tourism to the GDP of five regions in 2018, as a percentage, led by the Maldives at 38.92 per cent.

Table 2 shows the percentage of people engaged in tourism in five regions in the same year, led by Aruba at 29.91 per cent.

So one table measures tourism's share of the economy and the other its share of employment. Both are drawn from World Bank data.

Not quite. Three regions appear in both tables: Aruba, Macao and Seychelles.

Table 1 also names the Maldives and the British Virgin Islands, which do not appear in Table 2; Table 2 also names St. Lucia and The Bahamas, which do not appear in Table 1.

The overlap is what matters. A region can earn a large share of its GDP from tourism without employing a correspondingly large share of its people, and the reverse, so the two measures rank the regions differently even where the same places appear.

Because these are small island economies with little else to live on, and with exactly the conditions that draw visitors.

The chapter says so directly: looking at the countries given in the table, most of these regions are island countries, and therefore the climate, the natural beauty of the region, the availability of land and sea adventure sports make tourism a major contributor to the country's GDP, and the population employed in tourism is higher.

The share is high partly because the denominator is small. An island has limited land, so primary activities are restricted, and a small domestic market, so large-scale manufacture is unlikely. What tourism earns therefore forms a large part of a small total.

The chapter adds the conditions such places must also have: advanced means of transport and the basic infrastructure facilities for tourism, without which natural beauty alone would bring nobody.

Tourism grows where a place is worth visiting and possible to visit, and the chapter divides the factors into physical and human on exactly that line.

The physical factors it names are the site and situation of a place, climate, relief, altitude, biodiversity, accessibility and availability of water. These decide what there is to see and whether people can be there comfortably.

The human factors are transportation facilities, lodging and boarding facilities, cultural diversity, government policies and the political conditions in a country. These decide whether visitors can reach the place, stay in it, and feel safe doing so. The chapter stresses advanced means of transport and basic infrastructure facilities in particular.

The tables show what follows when both sets are present in a small economy. The island regions listed have climate, natural beauty and land and sea adventure sports on the physical side, and the transport and infrastructure to make use of them, so tourism reaches 38.92 per cent of GDP in the Maldives and employs 29.91 per cent of the people in Aruba.

The reverse case completes the point: where accessibility, infrastructure or political stability is missing, tourism stays small however striking the scenery.

A divided (component) bar diagram is the suitable choice, because the three figures for each country add to 100 per cent and the question is how that whole is shared.

Draw the ten countries along the X-axis and percentage from 0 to 100 on the Y-axis. Draw one bar of equal height for each country, divided into three parts in the order primary, secondary, tertiary, with a different shading for each and an index. A multiple bar diagram, with three bars per country, would also serve if the aim is to compare one sector across countries rather than the share within each.

Interpretation.

The tertiary sector is the largest in every one of the ten countries, ranging from 37.9 per cent in Tanzania to 77.4 per cent in the U.S.A. That alone is the chapter's point that tertiary activities are expanding day by day.

The countries divide into two groups by their primary share. Denmark, the United Kingdom and the U.S.A. stand at 1.0 per cent, the Russian Federation at 3.0 and New Zealand at 7.0; Kenya stands at 34.0, Tanzania at 29.0, Uganda at 24.0, Tajikistan at 21.0 and India at 14.0. The first group are developed economies, the second still largely agricultural.

The tertiary share follows the same split in reverse. The five countries with the smallest primary shares carry tertiary shares of 54.0 to 77.4 per cent, while Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Tajikistan carry 37.9 to 47.6.

The secondary share separates the two groups least. It runs from 21.6 per cent in the U.S.A. to 43.0 in the Russian Federation, and a developed and a developing country can share almost the same figure: Denmark 34.0 and Tanzania 33.1.

The conclusion is that the proportion between the sectors, rather than any one of them, indicates a country's stage of development, and that the primary share is the sharper discriminator of the three.

All the main kinds the chapter names will occur here.

Trade, because the countries produce different things. The index shows horticulture, fruit, rice, coffee, tea, fish and forest produce distributed among the five, and the chapter's first factor in trade is that the natural resources available in one country differ from those in another.

Transport, by sea through the ports the index marks, along the river that crosses the land, and by road and rail between the countries.

Loading and unloading of goods, which the chapter lists among tertiary activities and places at ports and dockyards.

Wholesale and retail trade within each country, since the chapter notes that markets always occur near settlements.

Communication, banking and insurance, all of which the chapter lists among tertiary activities and all of which international trade requires.

Tourism is likely too, given the coast, the river and the forest.

Country E is landlocked, so it has no port of its own and must trade through its neighbours.

Its goods will move overland, by road or rail, to a port in one of the coastal countries and be shipped from there, and its imports will arrive the same way in reverse. The river shown on the map could serve the same purpose where it is navigable.

That makes E dependent on its neighbours in a way the others are not. It must keep good relations with them, which the chapter touches on when it says a country may carry out trade with another to maintain good relations, and its costs will be higher because every consignment is handled twice and carried further.

Air transport is the alternative for goods that can bear the cost. The chapter notes that with the development of technology air transport is now used more, but that major trade still happens through ocean routes, and that airways suit high-value or perishable goods, as with the grapes it gives as an example.

The map shows geography deciding what each country does and how it can trade.

What is produced follows the physical setting. The countries with forest carry forest produce, those with suitable land and climate carry tea, coffee, rice, fruit and horticulture, and those on the sea carry fish. The chapter's account of trade makes this its first factor: each region differs from another, and soil, minerals, forests, land and water are unevenly distributed, so a country rich in soil is a good exporter of grains while one that cannot farm on a large scale must import them.

Climate decides the difference more finely still. The chapter notes that climate ensures how different types of products can be grown, and that is why tea and coffee appear in some of these countries and not others.

Location decides how the produce moves. The four coastal countries have ports and can ship directly; country E, being landlocked, must send its goods overland through a neighbour. The chapter's treatment of transport says coastal locations are favourable for the development of ports and harbours, especially broken coastlines, and that not all coastal areas can be good ports.

The river shapes both. It waters the land it crosses, which is why cultivation appears along it, and it offers a route inland.

Taken together the map makes the chapter's case that the foundation of trade lies in geography: the differences between these countries are natural, and it is those differences that give them something to exchange.

| A | B | C |
|---|---|---|
| 1) Matheran | Tourism | Tertiary Activity |
| 2) GPS | Satellite | Communication |
| 3) Sri Lanka | Tea | Export |
| 4) Panama Canal | Atlantic Ocean | Pacific Ocean |

Each chain runs from a place or thing, through what it is associated with, to what that belongs to or connects.

Sri Lanka and the Panama Canal come straight from the chapter. It states that Sri Lanka is a major tea exporter country, and that the Panama Canal joined the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.

GPS chains through the satellite to communication, and the chapter says the satellites in space work for communications day and night.

Matheran is a hill station, so it chains through tourism, which the chapter treats as one of the tertiary economic activities.

Because the sector is defined by what it does between the other two, and that is of both kinds.

The chapter describes tertiary activities as those which act as the link between the primary and secondary activities and are complementary to both, mostly in the form of services, adding that if you want a particular service you have to pay for it.

The list it then gives contains both halves. The exchange half is buying and selling of goods, marketing, and import and export. The service half is means of transportation and communication, loading and unloading of goods, credit facilities, public services, and others such as knife grinders, vegetable sellers, shopkeepers, passenger carriers and postal services.

The two are hard to separate in practice. An exchange cannot happen without transport to move the goods, banking to pay for them and communication to arrange them, so the services exist for the sake of the exchange and the exchange depends on the services.

Because air transport does what no other mode can, and technology has made more of it possible.

The chapter states that with the development of technology air transport is now used more, while noting that major trade still happens through ocean routes.

Speed is its advantage, and for some goods it is decisive. The chapter's own example is that for international export of a product like grapes, obtained through agriculture, using airways will be a better option, while sending cotton through water transport will be more profitable. Perishable and high-value goods can bear the cost of flying; bulky low-value ones cannot.

The chapter's other example makes the same point from the grower's side: flowers for the Gulf countries can remain fresh and retain their quality because those countries are within the reach of an hour or two by air.

Air transport is also the only mode not stopped by relief. The chapter notes that dense forests and hilly and mountainous regions affect the construction of long route rails and roads, whereas an aircraft passes over them; what it needs instead is a favourable climate, advanced technology and plain regions for airports, with constant fog or smog and areas of high peaks as its obstacles.

Because trade exists only where one place has what another lacks, and it is geography that makes places differ.

The chapter puts it plainly: it may occur to you that this is an economic concept, then why are we discussing this in geography? But actually the foundation of this activity lies in geography.

Its first factor is difference in natural resources. The concept of a natural region specifies that each region is different from another, and soil, minerals, forests, land, water and human resources are unevenly distributed, so what is abundant in one country is scarce in another. A country rich in soil will be good in agriculture and may export grains, while one that does not farm on a large scale must import them; the Gulf countries, rich in mineral oil, export oil and import grains.

Its second is climate, which affects the plants and animals of a region and decides what can be grown or produced. Snow-covered countries export meat and woollen products; tropical countries export bananas, rice, cocoa, tea and coffee. Sri Lanka's cheap labour, favourable climate, undulating land and well-draining soil make large-scale tea plantations possible, and it produces more tea than its population requires, while the United Kingdom has no plantations and a high demand, so tea moves from one to the other.

If every region had the same resources and the same climate, there would be nothing to exchange.

The chapter treats satellites as the means by which modern communication reaches everywhere at once.

It notes that the use of technology in communication has increased manifold, giving satellites as its example, and that the satellites in space work for communications day and night.

Their importance lies in what they overcome. Landlines and cables must be laid across the ground, so relief, distance and terrain limit them in the way the chapter describes for rails and roads. A satellite signal is not stopped by a mountain, a forest or an ocean, so it can serve places no cable reaches.

Satellites also carry far more than messages. GPS, which the chapter's own exercise chains to the satellite and to communication, gives position anywhere on earth, and satellite imagery is used in the practical work of geography itself.

The chapter places communication alongside transportation in its classification of tertiary activities, and satellites are what allow a trade arranged in one country to be settled in another the same day.

Trade cannot happen without transport, and the chapter says so directly: transportation is a very important tertiary activity for trading, and the importance of ports, sea transport and air transport has been very obvious in trade.

Transport decides what can be traded at all. The chapter notes that the mode of transport matters as much as how long a perishable raw material will last, and gives the comparison: for international export of grapes, airways will be a better option, while sending cotton through water transport will be more profitable. A perishable good without fast transport cannot be traded over any distance.

It also decides the routes trade takes. The chapter observes that although air transport is now used more, major trade still happens through ocean routes, and that two canals changed the course of transport radically, the Suez Canal connecting Asia with Europe and Africa, and the Panama Canal joining the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, both built to avoid long ocean routes.

It decides where trade is handled. Loading and unloading of goods takes place at ports and dockyards, and the chapter observes that such places are located near water transport or airways.

And it limits who can trade. Coastal locations favour ports, especially broken coastlines, but not all coastal areas can be good ports, so a country's access to trade is partly settled by its coast.

Tourism can form a large part of a country's national income, and in some it forms the greater part of it.

The chapter's table shows the direct contribution of travel and tourism to GDP in 2018: the Maldives 38.92 per cent, the British Virgin Islands 32.96, Macao 28.01, Aruba 27.64 and Seychelles 25.73. A second table shows the share of people engaged in tourism, led by Aruba at 29.91 per cent.

The chapter explains the pattern: most of these regions are island countries, and therefore the climate, the natural beauty of the region and the availability of land and sea adventure sports make tourism a major contributor to GDP, with a correspondingly high share of the population employed in it.

The contribution is high partly because these economies are small. An island has limited land for primary activities and a small home market for manufacture, so what tourism earns is a large share of a small total.

A high share also means a high risk, since an economy resting on one activity is exposed to anything that stops visitors coming. That is part of why the chapter's passage on tourism planning insists that planning is necessary for the sustainable development of a destination.

| Point of difference | Secondary economic activities | Tertiary economic activities |
|---|---|---|
| What they do | Transform raw materials into goods; products are processed to make them usable, more durable and saleable at higher prices | Provide services, and act as the link between primary and secondary activities |
| What they depend on | Products obtained from primary activities | Neither derives from nature as primary does, nor mainly produces goods as secondary does |
| Output | A new and different physical product | A service; any product made is in the form of a service offered |
| Also known as | Manufacturing, processing and construction industries | The service sector |
| Where the work is done | In a factory, the place where products of primary activities are converted into final products | Wherever the service is wanted, and for markets always near settlements |
| Freedom of location | A secondary activity can occur away from the settlements | Markets will not; they are always found near settlements |
| Examples | Sugar mills, cotton textile mills, iron and steel works, bakeries | Buying and selling of goods, transport, communication, loading and unloading, credit facilities, marketing, import and export, public services, tourism |

| Point of difference | Quaternary activities | Quinary activities |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of the work | To think, research and develop ideas | Work of an administrative character |
| Sectors involved | Education, information, research and development | The highest levels of administration and management |
| Examples | Financial planners, tax consultants, software developers, statisticians, people working in offices, hospitals and theatres, school teachers, university professors, accountants | Senior business executives, government officials, scientists, judges |
| The distinguishing point | They produce and apply knowledge | The people involved are engaged in the highest level decision-making or policy-making |

The chapter presents both as specialised services split off from the tertiary sector, because the services in that sector are varied in nature and have a very vast coverage. Its summary diagram places them as the fourth and fifth stages: primary produces raw materials, secondary transforms them into goods, tertiary provides services, quaternary is research, training and teaching, and quinary is decision-taking and policy-making.

| Point of difference | Waterways | Airways |
|---|---|---|
| Medium | Water | Air |
| Speed | Slow | Fast |
| Cost | Cheap, so suited to bulky low-value goods | Costly, so suited to high-value or perishable goods |
| Suitable cargo | The chapter's example is cotton, which is more profitable to send by water | The chapter's example is grapes, for which airways will be a better option |
| Share of trade | Major trade still happens through ocean routes | Now used more with the development of technology, but still the smaller share |
| What its development needs | Coastal locations, especially broken coastlines, for ports and harbours; not all coastal areas can be good ports | A favourable climate, advanced technology and plain regions for airports |
| What obstructs it | The length of ocean routes, which is why the Suez and Panama Canals were built | Constant fog or smog, and areas with high peaks |
| Effect of relief | Not affected by relief on land | Not affected by relief in flight, only at the airport |

The chapter begins by defining what trade is: the voluntary exchange of goods and services in which two or more parties are involved. The barter system was its initial form among primitive societies, with only an exchange of goods; today trade occurs in goods and services, within a country as well as between countries, and bilateral and multilateral trade are the major types of international trade.

It then states the condition under which international trade happens at all: it occurs when it is mutually beneficial to trading partners and when it is a comparative advantage for both, rather than producing in their own countries. It is a result of specialisation in production and human resources.

The geographical factors affecting it are five.

Difference in natural resources. Each natural region differs from another, and soil, minerals, forests, land, water and human resources are unevenly distributed, being abundant in one region and scarce in another. A country rich in soil will be good in agriculture and may export grains, while a country that does not practise agriculture on a large scale must import them. The Gulf countries, rich in mineral oil, export oil and import grains.

Climate. Climate affects the plants and animals in a region and ensures what can be grown or produced. Countries snow-covered for a major part of the year export meat and woollen products; tropical countries produce and export bananas, rice, cocoa, tea and coffee. Sri Lanka is a major tea exporter, because cheap labour, a favourable climate, undulating land and soil which can drain water make tea plantations possible on a large scale, and its production exceeds what its population requires. The United Kingdom has no tea plantations but a high demand, so India and Sri Lanka export tea to it.

Population factors. The size, distribution and diversity of people differ between countries.

Specialisation. Some countries have specialised goods and services; Israel has specialised in dry farming or agricultural engineering and exports those services to countries wishing to farm in desert-like conditions. Specialised goods and services have an international demand, so trade may occur.

Government policies. These may cause or stop international trade. A free trade policy will not restrict citizens from buying or selling to another country, and a country may trade with another to maintain good relations.

To these the chapter adds transport, treated under a heading of its own, since the importance of ports, sea transport and air transport has been very obvious in trade.

The chapter names relief, location and climate as the three major physical factors governing the development of transport, and shows each at work.

Relief. It is generally easier to build rails, roads and pipelines where relief is not rugged. Dense forests and hilly and mountainous regions affect the construction of long route rails and roads, and the chapter gives the dense forest and arid regions of Africa and South America as places where building long distance roads and rails is difficult.

Location. Coastal area locations are favourable for the development of ports and harbours, especially broken coastlines. But the chapter immediately qualifies it: not all coastal areas can be good ports, so a coast is a necessary and not a sufficient condition.

Climate. For airways to develop one needs a favourable climate, and constant fog or smog becomes an obstacle to air transportation, as do areas with high peaks. Airports also need plain regions to be built on, which brings relief back into the account.

The chapter adds that each mode has its own requirements and features and is adapted to serve the specific demands of freight and passenger traffic, which gives rise to marked differences in the way these means are deployed and utilised in different parts of the world.

Geography can also be altered where the cost is worth it. Two canals changed the course of transport radically: the Suez Canal, connecting Asia with Europe and Africa, and the Panama Canal, joining the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, both constructed to avoid long ocean routes.

Because nothing a country produces is of use until it can be moved, and transport is what moves it.

The chapter defines transportation as a service or facility through which passengers and freight are carried from one place to another, and calls the means of transportation essential components of transport systems.

It makes trade possible. Transportation is a very important tertiary activity for trading, and the importance of ports, sea transport and air transport has been very obvious in trade. Without it a surplus in one region cannot meet a want in another, which is the whole basis of trade.

It decides what can be produced for sale. The chapter notes that the mode of transport matters as much as how long a perishable raw material will last, and that for international export airways suit grapes while water transport suits cotton. A perishable crop has no export market until fast transport exists.

It governs where industry can be. In the chapter on secondary activities, low cost of transportation is called the key factor in the location of industries.

It binds settlements and markets together. Markets always occur near settlements, and loading and unloading of goods takes place at ports and dockyards located near water transport or airways.

And it opens regions that would otherwise stay closed. Where relief makes long route rails and roads difficult, as in the dense forest and arid regions of Africa and South America, development is held back; where canals such as Suez and Panama shortened the ocean routes, trade was changed radically.

Tertiary activities are expanding because the services they consist of are needed in ever greater number, and because the sector keeps taking in new kinds of work.

The chapter's own table of national income shows the result. In 2018 the tertiary sector was the largest of the three in every one of ten countries listed, from 37.9 per cent in Tanzania to 77.4 per cent in the U.S.A., with the United Kingdom at 70.5 and New Zealand at 65.6.

The first reason is that the other two sectors depend on it. Tertiary activities act as the link between primary and secondary activities and are complementary to both, so as production grows, the buying and selling, transport, loading and unloading, credit, marketing, import and export that carry it must grow too.

The second is technology. The chapter notes that the use of technology in communication has increased manifold, giving satellites that work for communications day and night, and that with the development of technology air transport is now used more. Each advance creates services that did not exist before.

The third is that new services keep being recognised. The chapter observes that the services included in this sector are varied in nature and have a very vast coverage, and that some specialised services are now categorised into quaternary and quinary activities, covering education, information, research and development, and the highest levels of decision-making.

The fourth is rising demand. Tourism, which the chapter treats at length, contributes 38.92 per cent of GDP in the Maldives, and services such as banking, insurance, real estate and professional services grow as incomes rise.

The chapter's summary diagram captures the direction: primary produces raw materials, secondary transforms them, tertiary provides services, and beyond them lie research and policy-making, which are services too.

Mark either the Suez Canal, which connects Asia with Europe and Africa, or the Panama Canal, which joins the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans.

Show it with a distinct symbol and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

The chapter names both and explains why they qualify: two canals which changed the course of transport, the Suez Canal and the Panama Canal, were constructed to avoid long ocean routes, and they changed the use of ocean routes radically.

[Note: the chapter gives what each canal connects but not the seas or lands on either side of it, so locate the two canals from an atlas and mark them by the connection the chapter states.]

Mark a railway that runs continuously from one continent into another, that is a line crossing from Europe into Asia.

Show it as a line with a distinct symbol and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

[Note: the chapter discusses railways only in general terms, as one of the land means of transport whose construction is easier where relief is not rugged, and it names no intercontinental railway anywhere. The line to be shown must therefore be identified from an atlas. What the chapter does settle is the criterion: the railway marked must run without a break from one continent into another.]

Mark an international airport in India, for example at Mumbai or Delhi.

Show it with an airport symbol and enter it in an index in a corner of the map.

The chapter's conditions for air transport explain where such an airport can be: airways need a favourable climate, advanced technology and plain regions for airports, while constant fog or smog and areas with high peaks are obstacles. It also names the Delhi International Cargo Terminal among the places where loading and unloading of goods takes place, noting that such places are located near water transport or airways.

[Note: apart from the Delhi International Cargo Terminal, the chapter names no Indian airport, so the airport chosen should be taken from an atlas.]

Because tourism is not a single industry and its effects are not all good.

The passage says the need for planned development is of great importance in the tourism sector because it involves many industries working together in a complex way and needs special attention.

The passage calls communities the basic elements of tourism, and says tourism mainly depends upon the level of acceptance shown by local communities.

Because of that, their involvement in the process of planning is essential. A destination cannot be developed against the wishes of the people who live in it.

They are also the people the impacts fall on. The passage says the development of tourism creates impacts on the environment, the socio-culture and the economy of the host community, so the community both shapes the plan and bears its consequences.

Two benefits the passage names are these.

It makes the best use of limited resources. Planning tries to allot limited resources between various competitors with a view to maximising output, income and employment, and to making sure different sectors have fair growth. Without it, one sector could take resources at the expense of others.

It makes development sustainable. Planning is necessary to reduce the negative impact and boost the positive impact of tourism on the environment, the socio-culture and the economy of the host community, so that a destination can keep drawing visitors rather than being spoilt by them.

A third, if one is wanted, is that planning is the process through which the set goals can be achieved and the various choices linked to tourism development can be addressed.

Tourism itself does. The passage states that the development of tourism creates impact mainly on the environment, the socio-culture and the economy of the host community at any destination, and that these impacts produce both negative as well as positive impacts.

On the positive side the passage points to output, income and employment, which planning aims to maximise, and to fair growth across different sectors.

On the negative side it points to the impacts that planning exists to reduce, though it does not itemise them.

The community's own attitude matters too, since the passage says tourism mainly depends upon the level of acceptance shown by local communities, so an unwilling community limits what tourism can earn there.

Because a destination is never finished. The passage describes tourism planning as a long term and constant process of preparing, upgrading and improving a destination for the tourist.

Each of those three words points to a different stage, and the last two never end: preparing happens once, but upgrading and improving must continue as visitors' expectations, transport and competing destinations change.

It is long term also because of what it must balance. Planning allots limited resources between various competitors and makes sure different sectors have fair growth, and it works through many industries that operate together in a complex way, none of which can be adjusted quickly.

Finally, its aim is sustainable development, which by its nature is measured over a long period: the negative impacts on environment, socio-culture and economy accumulate slowly, and so do the remedies.
